 Federal judge awards restitution on 5% of $1M student loan scam
 By Michael Karlik 
 Published November 2, 2026 1:04pm 
 + Add Colorado Politics on Google 
 Regina M. Rodriguez during her confirmation hearing for a U.S. District Court judgeship. (CQ-Roll Call/pool) 
 A federal judge last month ordered that a pair of defendants pay crime victim restitution on only 5% of the estimated $1 million student loan fraud they orchestrated.
 Between 2018 and 2021, Jalon Torres of Colorado Springs falsely promised people with student loan debt that they could obtain reductions or forgiveness through his company, the Student Resolution Center, LLC. He obtained authorization to withdraw payments from victims’ bank accounts. Instead of paying off student loans, Torres and co-defendant Lisa Marie Ritter used the money for themselves.

 Earlier this year, the government reached agreements with both defendants, with Torres agreeing to plead guilty to wire fraud and money laundering. Ritter would plead guilty to concealing a felony.
 Both plea bargains referenced that the Student Resolution Center received $1 million in payments. Ritter’s plea bargain also indicated she agreed to pay restitution, “which is estimated to be approximately $1 million.”
 Shortly before the sentencing in July, the government asked for a separate restitution hearing because it needed more time.
 “The financial analysis conducted in this matter is highly extensive. The defendants engaged in a scheme to defraud over 1,300 student loan debtors by making materially false promises regarding loan reduction or forgiveness in exchange for a set number of payments,” wrote the U.S. Attorney’s Office. Because the defendants’ scheme involved checks that would bounce or be reversed, “it is challenging to attribute a particular bounced check or reversal to a particular victim on SRC LLC bank statements. This makes each victim’s final loss amount difficult to ascertain from SRC LLC bank statements alone.”
 Then, on Oct. 15, the government submitted its motion for restitution in the amount of $54,301.59, roughly 5% of its original estimate.
 For the past four months, “the Government has been diligently attempting to contact all known victims to ensure that every victim has been notified and given ample opportunity to claim restitution in this matter,” the U.S. Attorney’s Office wrote. “The Government has made such attempts by letter, email, and by phone. Any time a letter has been returned or an email bounced back, the Government has searched for updated contact information and attempted to make contact again.”
 Although many victims responded, “many more have not,” the motion continued.
 The government listed only the financial losses that were supported by documentation and for which the victims had made claims under penalty of perjury. Neither the defendants nor the probation office opposed the amount.
 On Oct. 20, U.S. District Court Chief Judge Regina M. Rodriguez formally imposed the requested amount. 
 “Although this restitution amount is less than the Probation Office and Government predicted,” she wrote, “the Government’s process in determining the amount and documentation comply with (the restitution law).”
 The case is United States v. Torres et al .
